analysis.one_liner: Loosens post-2008 banking rules, freeing smaller banks, insurers, and mortgage lenders from parts of Dodd-Frank oversight.
analysis.headline: The Senate Banking Committee's broad banking deregulation bill was reported to the Senate in June 2015, held three hearings, then sat on the Senate calendar for the rest of the Congress and never received a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill rolls back a wide set of banking rules put in place after the 2008 financial crisis. It would raise from $10 billion to $50 billion the asset size at which banks face direct Consumer Financial Protection Bureau supervision, exempt banks under $10 billion from the Volcker rule banning banks from trading for their own accounts, ease mortgage rules for manufactured-home sellers and lenders who keep loans on their own books, and bar regulators from the Justice Department's Operation Choke Point effort. It also adds some Federal Reserve transparency requirements. It cleared the Senate Banking Committee on June 2, 2015, and was placed on the Senate calendar, but the Senate never voted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Mid-size banks between $10 billion and $50 billion in assets would escape direct Consumer Financial Protection Bureau exams and reporting. Banks under $10 billion would be exempt from the Volcker rule's ban on trading with their own money. Insurance companies that control banks would get protection from FDIC claims and an affirmation that states, not Congress, regulate insurance rates. Manufactured-home retailers and their employees would be exempt from mortgage-originator rules, and lenders holding loans on their own books would get a shield from certain mortgage liability suits.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the CFPB examination and reporting threshold from $10 billion to $50 billion in assets, removing direct CFPB supervision of banks and nonbanks in that range.
Exempts banks and their holding companies with $10 billion or less in assets from the Volcker rule's prohibitions on proprietary trading and hedge fund relationships.
Extends the lighter 18-month on-site exam cycle to insured banks with up to $1 billion in assets, double the current cutoff, and directs agencies to develop short-form reporting forms.
Creates a safe harbor treating loans that lenders keep on their own balance sheets as qualified mortgages, shielding the lender from certain Truth in Lending Act liability.
Exempts manufactured and modular home retailers and their employees from the mortgage originator definition and loosens the high-cost loan thresholds that trigger extra protections.
Prohibits the FDIC, OCC, Federal Reserve, CFPB, and NCUA from implementing or participating in the Justice Department's Operation Choke Point initiative.

Requires the Federal Open Market Committee to explain its policy decisions to Congress quarterly, publish meeting transcripts within three years, and makes the New York Fed president a presidentially appointed, Senate-confirmed position.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers borrowing from banks newly freed from CFPB supervision would lose a direct federal examiner watching consumer compliance. Manufactured-home buyers would face weakened high-cost loan protections. Rules against banks trading with insured deposits would lapse for smaller banks. Privately insured credit unions could join the Federal Home Loan Bank System, shifting some risk onto that government-chartered system.

drawbacks.text: The mortgage safe harbor applies regardless of whether the loan is a balloon loan, and shields lenders from suit for failure to comply with the core ability-to-repay requirements, as long as the loan stays on the lender's books and basic borrower information is documented.

Raising the CFPB supervision threshold fivefold to $50 billion removes direct federal consumer-compliance oversight of a large tier of banks and nonbank lenders, the same threshold debate that resurfaced in later Congresses.

For manufactured homes, the bill raises the high-cost loan trigger from 8.5 to 10 percentage points and from $50,000 to $75,000, which means more expensive loans to lower-income buyers escape the extra disclosures and restrictions high-cost loans carry.

Exempting banks up to $10 billion from the Volcker rule allows insured depositories to engage in proprietary trading that current law bars, with only a safety-and-soundness backstop available to regulators.
The bill bars federal banking agencies from any participation in Operation Choke Point, ending a program aimed at payment processors serving high-risk merchants.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Some provisions are genuinely low-cost, such as streamlined exams for very small banks and added Federal Reserve transparency. But the core of the bill is regulatory relief for financial firms, and its consumer-benefit argument rests on the claim that rules like ability-to-repay and CFPB supervision restrict credit — a trade-off the bill does not measure, only study. The safe harbor, the fivefold CFPB threshold increase, and the manufactured-home threshold changes all move risk onto borrowers and, in the last case, onto the government-backed system. Weighed honestly, the bill's gains flow mainly to regulated firms while the protections it loosens exist for the public's benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was reported out of the Senate Banking Committee and placed on the Senate's calendar in June 2015, the committee held three hearings that July, and the Senate never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Senator Richard Shelby, chair of the Senate Banking Committee, introduced S. 1484 as an original committee measure and reported it to the Senate on June 2, 2015, the same day it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 103.
The bill lists zero cosponsors in the Senate.
The Banking Committee held hearings on the bill on July 8, July 16, and July 23, 2015, printed as S.Hrg. 114-103.
No further action appears in the record: the bill sat on the Senate calendar under General Orders and the Senate never voted on it before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The post-crisis rules the bill targeted — the $10 billion CFPB supervision threshold, the Volcker rule as applied to smaller banks, and the mortgage and manufactured-home lending protections — stayed in force. Banks, insurers, and mortgage lenders seeking that relief ended up no better off, while bank customers kept the existing oversight.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Bank customers; Dodd-Frank rules stayed intact

for.name: Richard Shelby
for.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced and reported the bill as an original committee measure on June 2, 2015, and chaired the committee hearings on it in July 2015.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote after it was placed on the calendar.

against.name: President Obama
against.what_they_did: Opposed rolling back Dodd-Frank protections and signaled he would veto legislation stripping key post-crisis financial rules.

sides.party_line_note: No committee or floor vote on the bill appears in the record; it was a Republican committee chairman's original bill with zero cosponsors, so support was never tested in a recorded vote.

industries.industry: Mid-size banks and lenders ($10–$50 billion in assets)
industries.note: The bill raises the CFPB examination and reporting threshold from $10 billion to $50 billion, freeing this tier from direct federal consumer-compliance supervision. Their gain comes at the cost of oversight of how they treat customers.

They get a Volcker rule exemption, longer exam cycles, short-form reports, and privacy-notice relief. Some of this reduces real compliance costs for community lenders, but the trading exemption removes a restriction on insured banks' speculation.

The bill affirms state-level insurance regulation under McCarran-Ferguson, exempts insurers that control banks from FDIC source-of-strength requirements, and limits FDIC liens when an insurer is liquidated. It reduces the federal backstop that protects policyholders and depositors.
The bill exempts retailers from mortgage-originator rules and raises the thresholds that define a high-cost loan, loosening oversight of financing sold to predominantly lower-income buyers.
Exemption thresholds for swap clearing become GDP-adjusted and indemnification requirements for clearing organizations and data repositories are repealed, easing post-crisis derivatives rules.

industries.industry: Federal Home Loan Banks and privately insured credit unions
industries.note: The bill lets credit unions whose deposits are not federally insured join Federal Home Loan Banks and access advances. That expands credit union funding but routes lending through the government-chartered FHLB system with only private insurance behind member accounts.
